questions.statement: "I live in Comayagua," she said. In other words, she said that she ___ in Comayagua.
questions.context: The present simple becomes the past simple in reported speech.

options.feedback: Correct! When the reporting verb is in the past, the present simple of the original shifts to the past simple.
Lives would keep the original present tense, which only happens when the reporting verb is also present.
The present perfect would suggest the living is relevant to now, and the shift from a past reporting verb requires the past simple.
A present continuous would be wrong because the shift applies to the tense of the original clause.

questions.explanation:
The rule of backshift: when the reporting verb is in the past, the tense of the direct sentence moves one step back. Present simple becomes past simple.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I finished the project," he said. She reported that he ___ the project.
questions.context: Past simple becomes past perfect in reported speech.

options.feedback: Correct! Backshifting a past simple event gives the past perfect.
The present perfect would be the result of backshifting a present tense, not of a past simple.
A past continuous would need an ongoing action in the original sentence, and finish is presented as complete.
Finishes is the original present form and has not been shifted at all.

questions.explanation:
Every tense moves one step further into the past: present simple to past simple, and past simple to past perfect. The reporting time and the original time no longer coincide.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She says she ___ in La Paz for three months.
questions.context: The reporting verb is present, so no backshift is needed.

options.feedback: Correct! With a present reporting verb the original tense is kept, and has been is the present perfect.
Had been is the backshifted form and is only correct with a past reporting verb such as she said she had been.
A future form would be the original tense only if the speaker had said will, and the time here is already past.
A present continuous would be the original only if she had used that form, and she did not.

questions.explanation:
Backshift depends on the reporting verb. She says keeps the present, and she said would force the past perfect. The choice of reporting verb decides the tense of the report.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I lost my pen," said Carlos. Carlos said that ___ had lost ___ pen.
questions.context: Pronouns and possessives change when a speaker is reported.

options.feedback: Correct! When the speaker reports his own words, the first person pronoun becomes third person and the possessive agrees.
Keeping the first person would make the report sound as if the reporter were the speaker.
The possessive must change with the person, so my cannot stay once the pronoun becomes he.
A plural pronoun would contradict the single speaker named in the original sentence.

questions.explanation:
Reporting someone else's words changes I to he or she, we to they, and my to his or her. The possessives always follow the new pronoun.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "This book is mine," said Ana. Ana said that ___ book was hers.
questions.context: Demonstratives change to point from the reporter's point of view.

options.feedback: Correct! This becomes that and mine becomes hers when the words are reported by someone else.
Keeping this and my would preserve the original speaker's point of view, which reporting removes.
These is the plural of this, and the original is singular, while our does not match hers.
Those is the plural demonstrative, and the sentence refers to a single book.

questions.explanation:
This becomes that and these become those in reported speech because the object is no longer near the reporter. Possessives shift in the same way: mine becomes his, hers or theirs.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He didn't say that he was tired. He said that he ___ tired.
questions.context: The verb say in a negative sentence, then reported.

options.feedback: Correct! A negative main verb is not backshifted; the negative stays in the report and the clause keeps its tense.
A past perfect would backshift a past simple, but was is a present form and the negative did not changes.
That would add a future meaning the original sentence does not contain.
A present perfect would shift the time reference to now, and the original was is a simple present.

questions.explanation:
The backshift applies to the tense of the reported clause, not to the negative auxiliary of the reporting verb. He didn't say that he was tired keeps the present simple.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I will meet her tomorrow at the square," he said. He said that he ___ meet her the next day at the square.
questions.context: Time and place words are adjusted in reported speech.

options.feedback: Correct! A future will becomes would when the reporting verb is in the past, and tomorrow becomes the next day.
Keeping will would ignore the past tense of the reporting verb said.
Be going to is a different future form and does not correspond to the will of the original sentence.
A past perfect would add two steps of backshift, which the original will does not require.

questions.explanation:
Will becomes would in reported speech, and the demonstrative time expressions shift as well: now becomes then, tomorrow becomes the next day, today becomes that day.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "She must be at the office," he said. He said that she ___ be at the office.
questions.context: A modal in reported speech, with a deduction.

options.feedback: Correct! Modal verbs have no past form of their own, so they stay unchanged in reported speech.
Had to expresses obligation in the past, not the deduction that must expresses in the original.
Should expresses expectation, and the deduction of must is stronger than that.
A must with have plus participle would refer to a deduction about the past, which the present must does not.

questions.explanation:
Modals and the auxiliaries do, does, did, have, is, are, was and were do not change form in reported speech. The meaning stays exactly the same as in the direct sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Are you coming?" she asked. She asked ___ she was coming.
questions.context: A yes or no question becomes an if or whether clause.

options.feedback: Correct! A polar question becomes a conjunction clause introduced by if, with the word order of a statement.
That cannot introduce a question with a yes or no answer, and the word order would also be wrong.
Which asks for a choice between named options, and the original question is polar.
What asks for the thing or the cause, not for a confirmation.

questions.explanation:
A polar question loses its question mark in reported speech. If replaces the auxiliary and the subject comes before it: she asked if she was coming.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Didn't you finish it?" he asked. He asked ___ she had finished it.
questions.context: The negative question reported as a negative clause.

options.feedback: Correct! Whether is the standard conjunction for reporting a polar question, and the polarity moves into the clause.
If not would need the negative inside the main verb, and the sentence already places not in the auxiliary.
That cannot introduce a question clause, and the reported content is a question.
Why asks for a reason, and the original question asks for confirmation.

questions.explanation:
Whether and if both introduce reported polar questions. Whether is more formal and is the one used before to or before a clause that needs or not.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Where do you live?" he asked. He asked ___ she lived.
questions.context: A wh question keeps its question word in reported speech.

options.feedback: Correct! A wh question keeps its question word and takes the word order of a statement.
If introduces polar questions, and a wh question needs its own question word.
Which asks for a choice between options, and the original question asks about a place.
What asks for a thing, and the original question asks about a location.

questions.explanation:
A wh question reports with its question word intact and the auxiliary after the subject. He asked where she lived is the standard pattern.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ me that he would be late for the meeting.
questions.context: The reporting verb tell, which requires a person as its object.

options.feedback: Correct! Tell takes a person as its object, and the past simple told is the past of tell.
Say does not normally take an indirect object, so said me that is not standard usage.
Speak cannot be followed by a that clause reporting someone's exact words.
Tells is the present form, and the sentence reports words already spoken in the past.

questions.explanation:
Tell plus a person plus the clause is the structure for relaying someone's words to a third party. Say plus a clause is used without naming the person told.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Close the window, please," she said. She said that I ___ close the window.
questions.context: A command reported with a to infinitive.

options.feedback: Correct! A reported command uses should plus base verb, which carries the obligation of the original imperative.
Must would express a stronger obligation than the polite request in the original sentence.
A future form would report a prediction, and the original was an instruction.
Be going to expresses an intention, which is not the meaning of an instruction given to someone else.

questions.explanation:
Imperatives do not shift tense because they have none. In reported speech they take should plus base verb, or a to infinitive after verbs like ask and tell.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I'll help you with the bags," he said. He said that he ___ help her with the bags.
questions.context: An offer or a suggestion reported in the past.

options.feedback: Correct! An offer with I'll becomes he would when it is reported in the past.
Keeping will would ignore the past tense of the reporting verb said.
A past perfect would backshift twice, and the original I'll requires only one step back.
A present continuous would describe an action under way now, which the original offer does not.

questions.explanation:
Offers and promises shift exactly like any other future: I'll becomes he would, and we shall becomes they would. One step of backshift is the rule.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I was cooking when he called," she said. She said that she ___ cooking when he called.
questions.context: A past continuous in the original sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! A past continuous normally stays as it is in reported speech, because there is no further past step for it.
A past perfect would change the meaning from an ongoing action to a completed one, which is a different report.
A future form would place the cooking after the call, reversing the original sequence.
A present perfect would link the cooking to the present, and the scene is entirely in the past.

questions.explanation:
Not every tense shifts. Past continuous, past perfect and modal verbs usually keep their form, because shifting them would change the meaning rather than the time reference.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I had already eaten," he said. He said that he ___ already eaten.
questions.context: A past perfect in the original sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! The past perfect is already the most backward tense, so it stays unchanged in reported speech.
A would have would add a hypothetical layer that the original plain statement does not contain.
A present perfect would move the eating towards the present, and the original is already in the past.
A future perfect would project forward from a future point, and the reporting verb is in the past.

questions.explanation:
The past perfect is the limit of backshifting. Once a tense is already the deepest past, reporting it in the past leaves it exactly as it was.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She didn't say she was ready. She said she ___ ready.
questions.context: Reporting the negative auxiliary of the reporting verb itself.

options.feedback: Correct! The negation stays in the reported clause and the tense of was is not shifted.
A past perfect would backshift a past simple, but was in the original is a present form.
Is not would keep the present tense, which is possible, but the sense of the report changes and was isn't correct.
A future negative would predict non-readiness, and the original was about a position already taken.

questions.explanation:
Negation does not move out of the reported clause. The reporter may say she didn't say, she said she wasn't or she denied it, and each version keeps the same tense inside the clause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Who did you speak to?" she asked. She asked ___ she had spoken to.
questions.context: A question with a preposition, where the preposition moves after the subject.

options.feedback: Correct! The question word who is kept and placed at the start of the reported clause, with the preposition to staying at the end.
In reported speech the preposition stays at the end of the clause, and to who is not a possible order in English.
If introduces polar questions, and this is a wh question that already has its own question word.
Which asks for a choice between options, and the original question asks about a person.

questions.explanation:
When a question begins with a preposition plus a question word, English reports it by moving the preposition to the end: who did you speak to becomes who she had spoken to.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "You must submit the form today," the teacher said. The teacher said that we ___ submit the form that day.
questions.context: A statement reported with a past modal obligation.

options.feedback: Correct! Modals keep their form in reported speech, and today becomes that day for the same reason.
Had to is a reasonable paraphrase, but the direct report of the original must keeps the modal unchanged.
Should would weaken the obligation into advice, and the original is a firm requirement.
A conditional modal would report a possibility rather than the stated requirement.

questions.explanation:
The tense of modals is fixed, but the time and place words still move. Today becomes that day and tonight becomes that night whenever the reporting verb is in the past.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "The results will be published on Friday," they announced. They announced that the results ___ be published on the following Friday.
questions.context: A statement about the future reported much later.

options.feedback: Correct! A future will reported with a past verb becomes would, and the day reference is adjusted to the next Friday.
Keeping will would treat the announcement as a present statement, and announced is in the past.
A past perfect would place the publication before the announcement, and the announcement comes first.
A present continuous passive would put the publication now, and the report is about a future event.

questions.explanation: A future passive shifts its first auxiliary: will be published becomes would be published. The passive part of the verb never changes, only the auxiliary in front of it does.
questions.subject: ingles
